newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda-Zaire border swamped by Hutu refugees.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda-Zaire border swamped by Hutu refugees.

text.p: A sea of Rwandan Hutu refugees as far as the eye could see streamed home from Zaire on Saturday along a newly found "road of hope".

The tide of refugees swamped the Goma-Gisenyi border post and the U.N. refugee agency said the Rwandan army had decided to close the frontier at 4 p.m. (1400 GMT) to control the influx. It was not immediately clear if they had brought down the barriers.
By Saturday afternoon, some 200,000 Hutus had crossed back into Rwanda since the reverse exodus began on Friday.

Despite the mass movement, involving at least one-third of the 1.1 million Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire, the United Nations still voted to dispatch a multinational humanitarian force to tend to their needs.
"The road of death is now a road of hope," said Ray Wilkinson of the UNHCR, adding the returnees were in good shape physically and seemed cheerful.
"It's pointless trying to count them. It's endless and we are running out of space every second," said a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Behind him a thick phalanx of refugees stretched into the distance, deep into Zaire, as far as the eye could see. Five-abreast, it moved across the horizon and into Rwanda.

The same mass of humanity crossed the border in chaos and panic in the opposite direction two years ago, fleeing victorious Tutsi rebels and reprisals for the anti-Tutsi genocide many of the Hutus had helped to commit.
This time the flood was peaceful but by Saturday afternoon, when the UNHCR said 200,000 people had crossed in less than 30 hours, the border post was swamped.
Rwandan soldiers and foreign aid workers abandoned plans for an orderly registration.
"The people decided to come back because they are tired, hungry and fed up," said Maurice Nsengrenwe, a 31-year-old former seminary student who fled Rwanda in 1994 with his Hutu kinsfolk.
Refugees in the Goma area of eastern Zaire began trekking home after the flight of Hutu gunmen who had persuaded or forced them not to go home.
The catalyst was a heavy bombardment on Thursday by rebels who now control eastern Zaire.

They shelled the area around Mugunga camp, makeshift home to about 400,000 Hutu refugees. The ex-Rwandan soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen -- chief culprits of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi minority -- lost their grip on the refugees.

"The Interahamwe told us in Rwanda there was no security so everyone was frightened but they have left and the rebels will chase them until even they are forced to come back," said one returning Hutu.
The sound of heavy machineguns boomed out west of Mugunga on Saturday as the rebels chased the Hutu fighters deeper into Zaire, Reuters correspondent Chrsitian Jennings reported.
The 15-member U.N. Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of a Canadian-led multinational force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reached refugees.
Canadian ambassador Richard Fowler said the refugee exodus did not obviate the need for a large number of troops.
"Close to a million refugees will remain at risk, even if the reports of current refugee flows into Gisenyi (Rwanda) are fully accurate," he added.
Rwanda said the refugee exodus meant the force was obsolete before it was even deployed and the world should send aid instead to help Rwanda settle the newcomers.

There were 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire before the month-long rebellion. Several hundred thousand are far to the south of Goma and there is no news of their condition or intentions.
About 540,000 Hutus chose exile in Tanzania in 1994 and the UNHCR said they were staying put so far.
The revolt in eastern Zaire, which groups ethnic Tutsis and other opponents of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, has also put hundreds of thousands of Zaireans to flight.
Zaire says it wants all the Hutus repatriated. But Zaire's ramshackle army may not have the power to force out the Hutu fighters determined to stay.
They face execution or years in prison for genocide crimes if they go home. Rwandan jails are already crammed with 80,000 Hutu genocide suspects.
Mobutu, an omnipotent ruler since 1965, has lost control of the east and there are rumblings of unprecedented discontent in many parts of Africa's second-largest country.
The Zairean leader has spent the past three months in Europe for treatment for prostate cancer and prolonged convalescence.
"He will soon return to Zaire to follow the operations which are unrolling in the field," Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told reporters after talks with Mobutu in France.
Zaire accuses the Tutsi military leaderships in Rwanda and Burundi of backing the rebels and occupying the east.
Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka promised "total war" to recover lost territory.
"We have lost the battle, not the war," said Zaire's army chief of staff General Eluki Monga.
